End-of-term reflections indicate limited prompting competence but growing confidence in applying subject-specific knowledge, although students often attributed unsatisfactory results to the LLM’s limitations rather than to their own prompt formulation. Challenges such as anthropomorphizing the models and overgeneralizing limited outcomes were also observed. The findings suggest that, in this specific classroom context, students reported engaging in metacognitive reflection while using LLMs, particularly when disciplinary knowledge was already well consolidated. However, limited knowledge of prompt design remains a major obstacle.

title: AI-generated versus human-developed assessment tasks in EFL context: insights from TPCK model
abstract: This study aimed to compare the pedagogical and content quality of AI-generated assessment tasks with those developed by humans in English language teaching, using a sequential-explanatory mixed-methods design. To accomplish this, 6 human-developed lesson plans from American English File 3 and 6 equivalent AI-generated lesson plans were analyzed. Twenty experienced EFL teachers were invited to evaluate and rate 52 assessment tasks from these lesson plans based on a TPCK-aligned rubric. Follow-up interviews were conducted to better understand the teachers’ ratings. Quantitative results showed no statistically significant differences between AI- and human-developed tasks across eight quality criteria. More specifically, teachers preferred AI-generated grammar and vocabulary tasks, while favoring human-developed reading, listening, writing, and speaking tasks. Moreover, qualitative analysis highlighted AI’s strengths in generating tasks quickly, providing a diverse range, and managing rule-based content. The study also emphasized the importance of teacher mediation to ensure personalization and contextual relevance. Overall, the findings emphasize the need for human-AI collaboration in EFL assessment design. In other words, AI tools are useful as initial resources rather than complete replacements for human-created assessments.

title: Exploring the viability of a framework for social justice-oriented digital transformation
abstract: This paper presents an application of a framework for educational social justice-oriented digital transformation, providing an analytical examination of four case studies of community-led design and implementation of digital technology with marginalized populations. The framework is rooted in a vision of social justice and reflects the principles of equity, inclusivity, participation and empowerment and ethical responsibility for marginalized populations. Through its five pillars - accessibility and infrastructure, inclusive pedagogy and curriculum, capacity building, ethical governance, and monitoring and evaluation – it is possible to see how the framework applies to the four cases. From this analysis, the framework is relevant in both analyzing previously implemented experiences of digital transformation and guiding new initiatives undertaken in practice through an educational social justice perspective.

title: Technology-enhanced inclusivity for educational ecosystems: Developing a framework for social justice-oriented digital transformation
abstract: This paper develops a framework for social justice-oriented digital transformation in educational ecosystems for marginalized populations. Following explanations of the concepts of digital transformation, justice-oriented transformation and digital ecosystems in education, challenges faced by marginalized populations are outlined. Two main components of the framework are highlighted: five core principles – equity, inclusion, participation by engaging marginalized communities in design processes, ethical responsibility guaranteeing transparency and accountability, and digital competence fostering empowerment and agency; and five pillars - accessibility and infrastructure, inclusive pedagogy and curriculum, capacity building, ethical governance, and monitoring and evaluation.

title: Capturing multidimensional engagement within small groups: A multimodal perspective
abstract: This study develops and validates a human-centered approach to measuring small-group, multidimensional engagement in a game-based Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) environment. Grounded in sociocultural perspectives, the proposed framework integrates multimodal data sources, including discourse, interaction logs, and linguistic indicators, to assess behavioral, collaborative, and disciplinary engagement through theory-informed human interpretation. Human-annotated engagement ratings serve as ground truth for evaluating whether supervised machine learning models can approximate multimodal interpretive judgments, establishing a pathway toward scalable assessment. Three supervised learning algorithms were compared to examine model performance across engagement dimensions, and multiple regression analysis was conducted to investigate associations between quest-level average engagement and group learning outcomes. Results indicate that average collaborative and disciplinary engagement ratings positively predict group performance, whereas behavioral engagement alone does not significantly relate to learning outcomes. Qualitative analysis of group responses further illustrates these associations. Methodologically and theoretically, the study advances multimodal learning analytics by proposing a generalizable, human-centered workflow that integrates multimodal interpretation with model-assisted scalability, emphasizing the essential role of human interpretation in producing valid and contextually grounded engagement assessments in collaborative learning environments.

title: AI-assisted, instructor-supervised grading and feedback in higher education: Design and evaluation of an end-to-end pipeline
abstract: This paper presents the design, deployment and evaluation of a GPT-4o-based grading and feedback pipeline for a Master’s-level Information Systems Project Management course, developed following the Design Science Research Methodology. The artefact orchestrates submission collection (Google Forms), rubric-based scoring with rubric-linked qualitative feedback (OpenAI GPT-4o via a Cloud Function) and analytics storage (BigQuery), across six consecutive case-study assignments. The AI grader supplemented rather than replaced instructor grading: official grades remained the instructor’s, while AI grades and feedback served as a second-opinion signal and additional formative feedback. The evaluation followed a pre-specified analysis plan combining a quantitative comparison of AI and instructor grades, a voluntary student survey and an automated assessment of feedback quality on the full corpus. Across 362 submissions from 66 students, the AI reproduced the instructor’s mark within the pre-specified tolerance of 0.5 points on a five-point scale in 83% of cases, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 points and a small systematic bias of −0.16 points (95% CI [ − 0.19 , − 0.12 ] ). Chance-corrected agreement, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), was moderate at best: ICC(2,1) = 0.49 (95% CI [ 0.33,0.61 ] ), spanning the poor-to-moderate range. Among the 112 survey responses (31% response rate), about 80% rated the feedback useful and 77% accurate. The pipeline operated at EUR 0.55 per student per assignment and delivered feedback within 24 h. The findings support using LLMs as scalable assistants for formative assessment, as a supplement to rather than a substitute for instructor evaluation.

title: The problem with defining teachers’ digital competency for deep learning: A rhetorical absurdity
abstract: This conceptual paper interrogates the mismatch between policy rhetoric and classroom practice concerning teachers’ digital competence for deep learning. The notion of rhetorical absurdity is used as a conceptual lens to describe the recurring contradiction between competency frameworks that promise technology-enabled deep learning and the persistent difficulty of translating these frameworks into situated educational practice. In this paper we synthesise literature across learning sciences, educational technology and teacher professional learning, and present contemporary technological constellations of Generative Artificial Intelligence and hybrid learning spaces as illustrations of the complexities with technology integration for deep learning. We argue that many teacher competency lists risk reinforcing a checklist mentality rather than enabling adaptive, epistemic and ethical capacities required for deep learning. We conclude with two rejoinders that explore shifts from static competencies to dynamic capability models with local translation into authentic educational settings. This multi-authored paper represents a joint intellectual effort originating from a working group convened at the UNESCO EDUsummIT 2025 in Dublin, Ireland.

title: Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics
abstract: Adaptive intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) are considered promising tools to address increasing heterogeneity in classrooms by tailoring instruction to individual learners. However, prior research often bundles multiple adaptive features, relies on non-equivalent instructional conditions, and predominantly focuses on older learners, limiting conclusions about specific adaptive mechanisms and younger students. To address these limitations, this field experiment investigated the isolated effect of task difficulty adaptation by comparing an adaptive and a non-adaptive ITS in early primary mathematics education among second-grade students ( N = 132). Both systems were identical in content, interface, feedback, and hints, differing only in the dynamic adaptation of task difficulty. We hypothesized that the adaptive system would outperform the non-adaptive system regarding students’ outcomes. Students engaged in a 30-minute training session, and pre-post assessments measured learning outcomes, cognitive load, and enjoyment. Additionally, an exploratory latent profile analysis based on motivational and cognitive learner characteristics examined differential effects. Results revealed no significant differences between conditions for learning outcomes, cognitive load, or enjoyment. Exploratory analyses indicated moderation by conscientiousness for subjective difficulty and enjoyment and differences in students' progression through the ITS. Learner profiles did not moderate the effects. These findings suggest that isolated task difficulty adaptation did not yield clear advantages over a non-adaptive system and highlight students' progression through the ITS and individual learner characteristics as promising targets for future research.

title: Corrigendum to “Technology-Enhanced Inclusivity for Educational Ecosystems: Developing a Framework for Social Justice-Oriented Digital Transformation” [Computers and Education Open 11 (2026) 100417]
Ethical principles of AI in education: Exploring teachers’ contextual ethical reasoning through an STS lens
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education (AIED) promises significant pedagogical transformations. However, it also raises concerns that have intensified global discourse on the ethical principles guiding its design and use. Despite this growing discourse, limited empirical evidence exists from the Global South, where little is known about how teachers in low-resource contexts conceptualize AI ethical principles. Addressing this gap, this study investigates in-service secondary school STEAM teachers’ conceptual understanding of Ethical Principles of AI in Education (EPAI-Ed). Guided by Socio-Technical Systems (STS) Theory, a two-stage qualitative design was adopted. Participants engaged in think-aloud (TA) protocols (n = 30) and follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 10). Data were analysed using sentiment coding and reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that, despite lacking formal training on AI ethics, teachers are not “ethics empty.” Instead, they rely on common sense and professional experience-based ethical reasoning shaped by professional identities, classroom realities, cultural norms, and contextual vulnerabilities to conceptualize and practice responsible AIED. This study provides novel insights into teachers’ ethical reasoning in low-resource contexts, addressing a critical gap in global AIED discourse. It also used the STS theory as an interpretive lens to explain how ethical reasoning co-emerges with socio-technical constraints. The findings offer practical implications for aligning teachers’ context-based ethical beliefs with global frameworks to mitigate AIED-related risks in educational spaces.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in elementary language education: A systematic review
abstract: Background Language acquisition during early childhood is foundational for cognitive, social, and academic development. While pedagogical theories have long guided early language education, the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at this level remains underexplored. Although AI has the potential to deliver personalized, adaptive, and engaging learning experiences, existing studies often lack theoretical grounding, generalize across educational phases, and overlook the developmental needs of young learners. As a result, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding how AI supports foundational language skills in authentic elementary education settings. Purpose This study conducts a systematic review, guided by the Diffusion of Innovation Theory, to address two research questions: (1) What are the main language education aspects addressed by AI in elementary education research? and (2) What are the predominant AI technologies and applications used, and how do they support language learning outcomes? The review maps current trends, identifies underrepresented areas, and offers practical insights for research, policy, and practice Methods Following PRISMA guidelines and guided by the PICOS framework, a structured search was conducted across six major databases to identify peer-reviewed studies published between 2013 and 2025. 31 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed through quantitative content analysis and thematic synthesis. Measures to reduce bias included dual independent screening, inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.75), and quality appraisal. Results Findings show a strong focus on speaking, literacy, and vocabulary, with limited attention to grammar, listening comprehension, and sign language. Pedagogical uses of AI centered on enhancing motivation, assessment, and personalized interaction. Conversational AI and natural language processing were frequently used, while advanced modalities like adaptive learning systems and biometric feedback were underutilized. Most studies employed qualitative or mixed methods with medium sample sizes and lacked grade-level specificity. Implications The review highlights the need for developmentally appropriate, pedagogically coherent, and ethically sound approaches to AI integration. It calls for research that addresses overlooked areas and adopts more rigorous methodologies. Policymakers must ensure ethical, inclusive, and equitable AI use in schools, supported by infrastructure investment and teacher training to maximise AI’s potential in elementary language education.

title: Navigating AI’s educational future: expert scenarios and implications for teaching and teacher preparation
abstract: This paper presents expert perspectives derived from a visioning activity conducted by an international panel of educational researchers from 13 countries and 18 institutions, working under Thematic Working Group 5 for UNESCO’s EDUsummIT 2025. Using a futures thinking approach, the experts co-constructed six scenarios imagining AI-enriched educational environments in 2030 across primary, secondary, technical, and higher education sectors. Reflexive thematic analysis of these expert-generated artefacts identified 12 cross-cutting themes. Three meta-patterns emerged: the more-human paradox, in which AI saturation intensifies rather than displaces human pedagogical work; the agency-scaffolding tension, in which student AI agency must be carefully developed rather than assumed; and contextual variation, in which the meaning of critical AI partnership differs across educational phases. Together, these meta-patterns suggest that pre-service teacher preparation moves beyond AI tool training to embed pedagogical rehearsal of scaffolding strategies that make effective use of GenAI's capabilities. We identify three priority areas that reflect the most pressing areas for action: (a) developing critical, agentic AI partnerships, (b) orchestrating AI-enhanced learning ecosystems, and (c) building trustworthy, equitable AI infrastructure. These insights aim to inform the design of teacher education and professional learning that is responsive to rapidly evolving AI-mediated educational environments.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for career guidance: A comparative analysis of computing competency recommendations across ten African countries
abstract: Employers increasingly expect graduates to utilize large language models (LLMs) in the workplace, yet the competencies needed for computing roles across Africa remain unclear, given varying national contexts. This study examines how six LLMs, namely ChatGPT-4, DeepSeek-V2, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3 70B, and Mistral AI 7B, describe entry-level computing career expectations across ten African countries. Using the Computing Curricula 2020 framework and drawing on Digital Colonialism Theory and Ubuntu Philosophy, content analysis of 60 LLM responses to standardized prompts reveals consistent coverage of technical competencies such as cloud computing and programming, but notable differences in non-technical competencies, particularly ethics and responsible AI use. Models vary considerably in their recognition of country-specific factors, including local technology ecosystems, language requirements, and national policies, with an average of only 35.4% contextual awareness overall. Two of the three open-source models demonstrate stronger contextual awareness and better balance between technical and professional skills, with Llama (4.47/5) and DeepSeek (4.25/5) outperforming proprietary alternatives ChatGPT (3.90/5) and Claude (3.46/5). However, Mistral's poor contextual performance (0.00/4) indicates that development philosophy alone (i.e., open source) does not guarantee contextual responsiveness. This first comprehensive comparison of LLM career guidance for African computing students uncovers entrenched infrastructure assumptions and Western-centric biases to varying degrees across all six models, creating gaps between recommendations and local realities. The findings challenge assumptions about AI tool quality in resource-constrained settings and underscore the need for decolonial approaches to AI in education, emphasizing contextual relevance and hybrid human-AI guidance models.

title: Roles for virtual reality integration into university teaching
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly integrated into university teaching, yet many VR projects lack clearly defined interdisciplinary roles. As a result, responsibilities remain unclear, collaboration becomes difficult, and technically sophisticated VR applications often fail to achieve their intended pedagogical outcomes. This study addresses this problem by identifying and structuring the interdisciplinary roles required for integrating VR into university teaching. Drawing on prior literature and 16 semi-structured expert interviews, we analyse how technological, pedagogical, and content-related knowledge is distributed across activities involved in VR integration. The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework serves to differentiate knowledge domains, while the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) provides a process-oriented perspective on when these knowledge contributions are required throughout development, implementation, and operation. Based on this analysis, we derive distinct interdisciplinary roles and corresponding team configurations, each characterized by core activities, primary knowledge contributions, and their position within the VR integration process. The resulting role descriptions operationalize the TPACK framework for VR integration in higher education and provide practical guidance for organizing interdisciplinary teams and implementing VR in a pedagogically sound manner.

title: Can AI help teachers? Experimental evidence on the effects of generative AI use and AI training on teachers’ lesson preparation
abstract: Teachers face considerable workload outside the classroom. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) could support teachers by enhancing lesson preparation while decreasing workload. Moreover, training on GenAI could further enhance its effectiveness and is increasingly demanded by practitioners. The present study examines whether GenAI (ChatGPT) effectively supports teachers during lesson preparation, and whether participation in AI training improves outcomes. For this purpose, we conducted a preregistered, RCT with N = 204 teachers who were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) No access to ChatGPT, (2) access to ChatGPT, and (3) access to ChatGPT with prior AI training. Teachers completed four incentivized lesson preparation tasks: Crafting an introductory quiz, writing a course mail, extending a textbook exercise and creating text and transfer questions. Dependent variables were (a) quality of the prepared materials, assessed by blinded expert ratings based on weighted criteria and (b) time spent on total preparation. Results indicated that GenAI effectively helped teachers during lesson preparation tasks, demonstrated by improved lesson preparation quality and a 34 % reduction in preparation time. AI training did not further improve lesson preparation quality but led to an additional 21 % reduction in preparation time. As revealed by prompt data, AI training led to a distinct prompt strategy (as intended): Teachers with prior training wrote longer and more detailed prompts, that needed less refinement afterwards. Untrained teachers used shorter prompts that required more subsequent prompt iterations. Although the first strategy required less preparation time, both strategies led to equal output quality.

title: Revisiting Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) development for the age of generative AI
abstract: This paper examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in K-12 education interacts with teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK). Using the Refined Consensus Model (RCM) as an analytical framework, we analysed how GenAI influences the three PCK domains: personal PCK (pPCK), collective PCK (cPCK), and enacted PCK (ePCK). Guided by the research question "How can teachers and GenAI collaborate to develop and use PCK and pedagogical reasoning in K-12?", we analysed three researcher-constructed vignettes – hypothetical but plausible scenarios representing GenAI use in planning, classroom interaction, and assessment – to derive analytical propositions about the PCK-GenAI relationship. Our analysis suggests tensions between traditional PCK boundaries and GenAI-mediated practices, particularly regarding the RCM's plan-teach-reflect cycle. We propose that GenAI can amplify teachers' PCK when critically evaluated, but poses risks for novice teachers whose pPCK is still developing. The paper identifies how GenAI reconfigures boundaries between personal and collective knowledge, reshapes enacted practice when AI becomes a co-constructor of teaching, and highlights the continued centrality of teacher expertise. We propose directions for supporting effective human-GenAI collaboration in PCK development and discuss implications for teacher education.

title: “I’m sorry, Dave. I’m afraid this feedback is not constructive”: Human perspectives versus ChatGPT evaluations of feedback in an era of artificial intelligence
abstract: Educators and scholars are contemplating the implementation of AI-generated feedback to enhance teaching and learning in various educational contexts. However, little is known about students’ beliefs about instructors’ use of AI-generated feedback, and the degree to which AI-generated evaluations of constructive feedback align with students’ perceptions. In a first study, we examined how ChatGPT evaluated human-generated feedback statements and compared these evaluations to human assessments of the same statements. We found unexpected discrepancies that led us to conduct a second study. Using a qualitative approach, we explored students’ perceptions of AI-generated feedback through focus group interviews, examining when their views of constructive feedback aligned or differed from ChatGPT output. Additionally, we investigated students' overall attitudes toward instructors' use of generative AI for providing feedback. Quantitative findings indicated that students’ perceptions of constructive feedback being specific and actionable were aligned with ChatGPT’s produced definition, but evaluations of timeliness and positivity diverged. Focus groups highlighted how instructor-generated feedback was valued for its relational, personalized, and expert-driven nature, whereas AI-generated feedback seemed impersonal to them and potentially unfair. Nonetheless, participants were open to hybrid feedback models, with instructors supplementing AI-generated feedback with their reading of students’ work. Our study underscores the nuanced tensions and opportunities in leveraging AI for educational assessment.

title: Motivational organization in AI-supported writing: A self-determination perspective
abstract: This study examined how students’ motivational regulation during creative writing was organized when generative artificial intelligence (AI) was unavailable or optionally available. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), motivation was conceptualized as configurations of intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, and external regulation. The sample comprised 406 students in Grades 5–8 who completed comparable creative writing tasks without AI (Time 1) and with optional AI access (Time 2). Using a micro-longitudinal, person-centered design, latent profile analyses identified motivational configurations and examined psychological need satisfaction and academic achievement as predictors of profile membership; degree of AI use was examined at Time 2. Mean levels of motivational regulation remained largely stable, whereas person-centered analyses revealed heterogeneity in regulatory configurations and differences in the prevalence of comparable profiles. Autonomy satisfaction declined at Time 2, while higher need satisfaction, particularly autonomy and competence, was associated with more self-determined configurations. End-of-term grades differentiated profile membership at both occasions. Degree of AI use did not significantly predict profile membership. Cross-context analyses showed correspondence alongside redistribution. Because full profile similarity was unsupported, these patterns were interpreted descriptively rather than as transitions between equivalent latent states. AI availability coincided with configurational differences not apparent from mean-level analyses. The findings distinguish AI availability from usage intensity and suggest that AI-supported writing should be understood in relation to psychological needs, academic functioning, and regulatory demands surrounding support, delegation, authorship, and agency.

title: Drivers and academic outcomes of generative AI use among university students in Benin
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education, offering potential gains in efficiency and quality, yet there are concerns about its cognitive and behavioral consequences. This study surveyed 633 university students in Benin to examine factors associated with GenAI use and its academic, behavioral and psychological outcomes. Drawing on the Expectancy Value Theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), we used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to assess how Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational sensitivities relate to GenAI use and its association with Academic Performance, Procrastination, and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Results show that Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational factors (Sensitivity to Rewards and Quality) were positively associated with GenAI use, which was widespread – more than 90% of students reporting use at least twice per week. GenAI use was positively associated with higher Academic Performance, but also with increased Procrastination and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Contrary to prior research, age, gender, and education level were not significantly associated with GenAI use, reflecting the widespread GenAI adoption across student groups. These findings highlight GenAI’s dual role as both a potential performance-support tool and a mechanism of cognitive offloading, underscoring the need for balanced integration strategies that leverage AI-assisted efficiency while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement and mitigating risks associated with overreliance on AI tools.
